Opus 5.5 inside Blender costs $4 per million input tokens, and it just beat a stack of specialist tools that charge by the seat

Price per seat hides the real comparison. One is a subscription per person, the other is a bill that scales with what you actually make.

> ASSET - a full set of product models built from one brief, geometry and materials included
> SHOT - the same products staged, lit and rendered across a dozen backgrounds
> COST - every tool’s output priced against what the run actually consumed

Photoroom and the rest are built around a photo. They cut, relight and restage something that already exists.

That ceiling shows up fast. No photo means no output, and a product that is not built yet has no photo at all.

Opus 5.5 starts earlier. The model is built in Blender, so every angle, every material and every background is a render away.

At $4 in and $20 out per million tokens, a full catalogue costs less than one seat of the specialist tools per month.

The quality gap is not subtle either. Real geometry holds up under lighting changes in a way a cut-out never does.

The brief, both outputs side by side and the full token bill are laid out underneath.

holy sh*t, Google Research just open-sourced an agent that can improve its own harness

steal this blueprint for a self-improving agent

the prompts, memory, skills and tool guidance around your model can evolve as it works

it’s called Harness²

the loop:

→ propose changes to the agent’s setup
→ run candidate setups on the same task
→ compare what actually happened
→ compose a refined harness from that evidence
→ carry useful lessons into future tasks

the clever part:

it refines the harness on unfamiliar tasks without a ground-truth answer to guide those edits

the architecture:

propose → probe → compose → retain lessons → repeat

the part builders should steal:

treat your agent’s setup as something you can experiment on

pick a recurring failure
propose a specific harness change
compare execution traces on the same task
evaluate the result
keep the evidence with the change

the repo includes OpenCode and Codex executors, parallel and sequential refinement, and a local demo you can run without model credentials

IT IS BECOMING F*CKING DANGEROUS. A 23-YEAR-OLD DEV FROM CHINA JUST RAN 300 GROK BOT RESEARCH AGENTS AT THE SAME TIME.

ANY TOPIC. RESEARCHED IN MINUTES. AND NONE OF THEM CAN LIE TO HIM.

These aren’t chatbots. Every single one is a research bot: it finds sources, pulls the facts and writes them up on any topic you give it.

He opens the live dashboard and it’s a rainbow of bots flying up the screen:

→ 300 Grok Bot research agents digging through sources at the same time
→ Every claim checked against the original source in ~100 ms
→ Three passes over 100 company profiles → zero errors left
→ Everything exported straight into a clean, structured database

The trick is the split.

Some of the bots do the research. The rest constantly check their work: they confirm every fact and decide whether it’s actually true. If they can’t find a confirmation or a source, they send the task back.

The loop doesn’t stop until every fact checks out.

That’s the part most people miss. More agents don’t make research better. A layer that refuses to accept unverified answers does.

Markets, competitors, people, products, science. Ultra-fast, accurate research on anything, without the usual AI guesswork.

An analyst team would bill weeks for this. He got it in one run, while the bots kept working on a cloud computer.

We’re moving from “ask AI a question” to “send a research swarm and only keep what’s proven.”

OpenAI got its own Pro reasoning mode wrong. They quietly corrected "GPT-6 Pro" to "GPT-6 Astra Pro". I spent yesterday digging through this confusing mess. fml.

What I figured out:
- GPT-6 Pro is powered by Astra, but Pro isn't simply another reasoning-effort level above Max.
- Pro is a reasoning mode, separate from reasoning effort (thinking level).
- ChatGPT's Pro selection switches model families. Instant through xhigh use GPT-6 Sol, while Pro uses GPT-6 Astra.
- Standard vs. Pro mode: Different execution configurations, not just different thinking budgets.
- Pro isn't necessarily better than Astra Max/Ultra on every task.
- Is Pro equivalent to Ultra thinking? No.
And don't confuse Ultra with Ultrafast.
- Many people assume Pro is just the same model thinking for much longer. That's incomplete.
- I'm already using Astra in Codex and Work. What GPT-6 Astra Pro adds in Chat is a different execution configuration and experience.

Pro can involve additional inference-time compute and orchestration, including parallel agents, rather than simply extending sequential reasoning. The exact reasoning budgets, agent counts, and aggregation mechanisms aren't disclosed. (why?)

Basically, extended thinking from the dinosaur era, now with orchestration ig.

From my testing:
ChatGPT Chat Pro use Astra with undisclosed reasoning effort and parallel agents. I've observed ~3 subagents working for roughly an hour for critical planning/spec (product design, sys arch), big discovery, and high-stakes work where mistakes have serious consequences. I can see the value. For basic research, Pro mode is overkill.

virals.text:
Anthropic, the company behind Claude, lost $80.7 billion in six months, according to its draft IPO filing. About $72 billion of that happened because the company got more valuable, and if its value had crashed instead, the same accounting rule would have booked it a gain on paper.

That sounds made up, so here's how it works.

When Anthropic raised money, a lot of it came in through convertible notes and similar deals. Think of them as IOUs that turn into stock later. Accounting rules make the company list those IOUs as something it owes, and price them at whatever that future stock is worth today.

Anthropic started 2026 valued at around $350 billion. It raised at $380 billion in February, and by late May it closed a $65 billion round at $965 billion, passing OpenAI. Every jump made those IOUs worth more on paper, and every time that happened the books recorded it as a loss, even though no actual cash went anywhere.

The same thing happened last year. Anthropic's 2025 net loss was $42 billion, and more than $34 billion of it came from this exact kind of adjustment, in a year when its value went from $61.5 billion in March to $350 billion by November.

Take the $72 billion out and you're left with a loss of about $8.7 billion over six months, on $16.3 billion of revenue. A year earlier, first-half revenue was $1.1 billion. Then Q3 by itself brought in $16.8 billion, more than the whole first half, and Anthropic told investors it was profitable on an adjusted basis that quarter.

The number I'd actually watch is somewhere else in the filing. Anthropic said it could spend as much as $750 billion on computing power over the next few years, and two customers made up about a fifth of its 2026 revenue. At last week's investor event, people reportedly talked about a valuation around $1.5 trillion, down from the roughly $2 trillion that was floating around for the November IPO.

Anthropic's IPO is going to come down to whether revenue growing 45% a quarter can keep up with a $750 billion computing bill.

outsiders.name: cedric
outsiders.text:
OpenAI got its own Pro reasoning mode wrong. They quietly corrected "GPT-6 Pro" to "GPT-6 Astra Pro". I spent yesterday digging through this confusing mess. fml.

What I figured out:
- GPT-6 Pro is powered by Astra, but Pro isn't simply another reasoning-effort level above Max.
- Pro is a reasoning mode, separate from reasoning effort (thinking level).
- ChatGPT's Pro selection switches model families. Instant through xhigh use GPT-6 Sol, while Pro uses GPT-6 Astra.
- Standard vs. Pro mode: Different execution configurations, not just different thinking budgets.
- Pro isn't necessarily better than Astra Max/Ultra on every task.
- Is Pro equivalent to Ultra thinking? No.
And don't confuse Ultra with Ultrafast.
- Many people assume Pro is just the same model thinking for much longer. That's incomplete.
- I'm already using Astra in Codex and Work. What GPT-6 Astra Pro adds in Chat is a different execution configuration and experience.

Pro can involve additional inference-time compute and orchestration, including parallel agents, rather than simply extending sequential reasoning. The exact reasoning budgets, agent counts, and aggregation mechanisms aren't disclosed. (why?)

Basically, extended thinking from the dinosaur era, now with orchestration ig.

From my testing:
ChatGPT Chat Pro use Astra with undisclosed reasoning effort and parallel agents. I've observed ~3 subagents working for roughly an hour for critical planning/spec (product design, sys arch), big discovery, and high-stakes work where mistakes have serious consequences. I can see the value. For basic research, Pro mode is overkill.

outsiders.name: Aakash Gupta
outsiders.text:
Anthropic, the company behind Claude, lost $80.7 billion in six months, according to its draft IPO filing. About $72 billion of that happened because the company got more valuable, and if its value had crashed instead, the same accounting rule would have booked it a gain on paper.

That sounds made up, so here's how it works.

When Anthropic raised money, a lot of it came in through convertible notes and similar deals. Think of them as IOUs that turn into stock later. Accounting rules make the company list those IOUs as something it owes, and price them at whatever that future stock is worth today.

Anthropic started 2026 valued at around $350 billion. It raised at $380 billion in February, and by late May it closed a $65 billion round at $965 billion, passing OpenAI. Every jump made those IOUs worth more on paper, and every time that happened the books recorded it as a loss, even though no actual cash went anywhere.

The same thing happened last year. Anthropic's 2025 net loss was $42 billion, and more than $34 billion of it came from this exact kind of adjustment, in a year when its value went from $61.5 billion in March to $350 billion by November.

Take the $72 billion out and you're left with a loss of about $8.7 billion over six months, on $16.3 billion of revenue. A year earlier, first-half revenue was $1.1 billion. Then Q3 by itself brought in $16.8 billion, more than the whole first half, and Anthropic told investors it was profitable on an adjusted basis that quarter.

The number I'd actually watch is somewhere else in the filing. Anthropic said it could spend as much as $750 billion on computing power over the next few years, and two customers made up about a fifth of its 2026 revenue. At last week's investor event, people reportedly talked about a valuation around $1.5 trillion, down from the roughly $2 trillion that was floating around for the November IPO.

Anthropic's IPO is going to come down to whether revenue growing 45% a quarter can keep up with a $750 billion computing bill.
